titleText.es: Yo iba a ser científico, pero ahora me parece una estupidez. Los mundos mágicos existen. He aprendido una gran verdad sobre nuestro lugar en el universo. ¿Se supone que me debe importar la universidad? JODER.
titleText.en: I was going to be a scientist, but that seems silly now. Magical worlds exist. I've learned a huge truth about our place in the universe. I'm supposed to care about college? I mean, FUCK.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text is the exact title attribute in the Spanish archive; the English text is the exact official xkcd title attribute.

applications.explanationEn: Ven is the irregular positive command telling one familiar person to come.
Ven supplies the action, while rápido stays in its masculine singular form and describes how the coming should happen.

regions.labelEs: HAS SALVADO NUESTRO REINO Y HAS HALLADO LA CONFIANZA EN TI MISMO. ES HORA DE VOLVER A CASA.

applications.explanationEn: Has supplies the present form of haber for tú, and salvado is the unchanged past participle paired with it.
Nuestro takes masculine singular -o because the owned noun reino is masculine singular.
Has supplies the present form of haber for tú, and hallado is the unchanged past participle paired with it.
Confianza names the confidence, en introduces its target, and ti is the form used for the person addressed after that preposition.
Ti is the form used for one familiar listener after a preposition, and mismo adds masculine singular self-emphasis.
Es hora de frames the moment to act, and volver remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
Volver supplies the return action, and a casa names home as the destination without an article before casa.
Llévate is the positive command telling one familiar person to take something along.
Te attaches to the positive command lleva, and the written accent preserves the original stress.
Para introduces the purpose, while recordar stays in its unchanged dictionary form inside recordarnos.
Nos attaches to the unchanged action recordar and identifies the people to be remembered.

regions.labelEs: VALE, SUPONGO QUE ME TOCA PASARME EL RESTO DE LA VIDA FINGIENDO QUE ESTO NO HA SUCEDIDO O SABER QUE TODA LA GENTE QUE QUIERO SOSPECHA QUE ESTOY LOCO.

applications.explanationEn: Me identifies the person whose responsibility it is, toca marks the assigned turn, and pasar remains in its unchanged dictionary form inside pasarme.
Me attaches to the unchanged action pasar and marks the speaker in the time-spending verb pasarse.

applications.exampleEs: PASARME EL RESTO DE LA VIDA FINGIENDO
applications.explanationEn: Pasarme marks the speaker, el resto de la vida gives the stretch of time, and fingiendo names the continuing activity in its -iendo form.
Ha supplies the present form of haber for a singular third person or thing, and sucedido is the unchanged past participle paired with it.
Estoy presents the speaker's condition, and loco supplies the masculine singular description.

regions.labelEs: VAN A SER 70 AÑOS MUY DIVERTIDOS.

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed age count is a numeral, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Van matches the plural time period treated as what lies ahead, a provides the link, and ser stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Divertidos follows años in the common neutral order for a description; muy separately strengthens the adjective.
Divertidos uses masculine plural -os to match masculine plural años; muy does not change.

cards.noteEn: Pringao is an informal, insulting spelling of pringado in which the d is dropped in speech. The feminine form is pringada.

example.en: Do not call him a loser.

cards.answerEn: pop; a sudden appearance sound effect
cards.noteEn: POP can imitate the abrupt sound of something appearing or opening. It is a sound effect, not the separate use of pop for a music genre.

cards.promptEs: portal fantástico · volver a casa · fingir que no sucedió
cards.answerEn: the joke follows a children's-fantasy triumph with the hero's bleak problem of returning to ordinary life
cards.noteEn: The familiar fantasy arc gives an insecure young person a magical mission, victory, and confidence, then sends him home. The last panel undercuts that empowerment: he expects decades of hiding an experience nobody else can verify.
Ven is the irregular positive command of venir, ‘to come,’ for tú, the familiar singular ‘you.’

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: verbo + adjetivo usado para describir el modo
cards.questionEn: How can words such as claro, alto, or profundo describe how an action is done without adding -mente?
cards.answerEn: In certain common combinations, put the describing word after the verb and keep it in its masculine singular form.
cards.noteEn: A word that normally describes a noun can sometimes work like an English -ly word and describe the action instead: hablar claro, volar alto, respirar profundo. It does not change for the person doing the action. This use is conventional, so it cannot be applied freely to every adjective.
Joven can be used on its own as a form of address rather than directly modifying a stated noun.

example.en: Excuse me, young person, can you help me?

cards.noteEn: As a reaction, joder can express anger, shock, pain, or frustration. It is common in informal speech in Spain but is strongly vulgar and unsuitable for polite situations.

example.en: Fuck, I have lost the keys!

cards.noteEn: The repeated a stretches the cry, and the final h is silent lettering that signals an exhaled scream rather than a dictionary word.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Salvado is the past participle of salvar. After a form of haber, it helps describe a completed action.

cards.questionEn: How do you choose the Spanish form of ‘our’ before a noun?
cards.answerEn: Choose nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, or nuestras to match the gender and number of what is owned.
cards.noteEn: The form matches the owned noun, not the owners. Use nuestro before one masculine thing, nuestra before one feminine thing, nuestros before masculine or mixed plural things, and nuestras before feminine plural things.
Hallado is the past participle of hallar. After a form of haber, it helps describe a completed action.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that confidence or trust is placed in someone or something?
cards.answerEn: Use confianza en, followed by the person or thing trusted.
cards.noteEn: Confianza names the confidence or trust, and en introduces its target. A word such as mi or su can say whose confidence it is, while a form of tener can say who has it.

example.en: We have confidence in the team.

cards.answerEn: in; required after confianza before the person or thing trusted
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses confianza en to introduce the person or thing in whom confidence or trust is placed.

cards.questionEn: How do you emphasize ‘myself,’ ‘yourself,’ or ‘themselves’ after a linking word such as en, para, or por?
cards.answerEn: After such a word, use mí, ti, or sí, then add a form of mismo that matches the person or people emphasized.
cards.noteEn: Words such as en, para, and por link what follows to another idea. Spanish uses mí for the speaker, ti for one familiar listener, and sí for a third person or formal listener after most such words. Mismo changes its ending to match, as in ti misma or sí mismos.
After a form such as mí, ti, or sí, mismo emphasizes that very person. Its ending changes to match: misma, mismos, or mismas.

cards.answerEn: it is (in an impersonal time expression)
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use es without a separate subject word in expressions such as es hora, “it is time.” English supplies the impersonal word “it.”

cards.promptEs: es hora de + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that it is time to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use es hora de, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Negation and contrast can surround the action: es hora no de discutir, sino de decidir.
After es, hora can identify the appropriate moment for an action rather than a clock hour.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links es hora to the action whose time has come
cards.noteEn: After es hora, use de before an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
Follow volver with de and a place or event to say where someone is returning from.

example.en: I have just returned from work.

cards.questionEn: How do you say to go home or return home?
cards.answerEn: Use ir or volver, then a casa, normally without an article before casa.
cards.noteEn: When casa means one's home as a destination, Spanish commonly leaves out la: ir a casa and volver a casa. The motion verb changes for the person and time; a casa remains unchanged.

cards.answerEn: take with you (an informal command to one person)
cards.noteEn: Llévate is the positive tú command lleva with te attached. Llevarse can mean to take something away with oneself; the accent preserves the original stress.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.noteEn: Recordarnos joins nos, meaning “us,” to the unchanged dictionary form recordar.

example.en: Keep the photo to remember us.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: to me; marks whose turn or responsibility it is
cards.noteEn: Before toca, me identifies the speaker as the person to whom the task falls.

example.en: It is my turn to pay.

cards.promptEs: tocarle a alguien + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action is someone's turn or responsibility?
cards.answerEn: Use a short recipient word such as me, te, le, nos, or les, then toca, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The short word identifies whose turn it is: me toca, te toca, le toca, nos toca, or les toca. The following action stays in its dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. A named person can be added with a, as in a Marta le toca.

example.en: It is our turn to clean the table.

cards.answerEn: is someone's turn; falls to someone to do
cards.noteEn: In tocarle a alguien hacer algo, toca does not mean physically touching. It says that an action is now that person's turn or responsibility.

example.en: Today it is my turn to cook.

cards.answerEn: to spend (a stretch of time), with me marking the speaker
cards.noteEn: Pasarme combines the unchanged form pasar with me. In pasarse + time + activity, it describes filling that period with the activity.

example.es: Voy a pasarme la tarde leyendo.
example.en: I am going to spend the afternoon reading.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone spends a stretch of time doing an activity?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching short word and a form of pasar, name the time period, then add the activity in its -ando or -iendo form.
cards.noteEn: The short word and pasar change with the person: me paso, te pasas, se pasa, nos pasamos. The final activity form describes what fills the time; it commonly ends in -ando or -iendo, as in leyendo, “reading.”

example.es: Lucía se pasa la tarde leyendo.

cards.noteEn: El resto names everything left after the already mentioned part has been separated out.

example.en: We will save the rest for tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; Spanish uses la before a general abstract idea such as vida
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses el or la when discussing an idea in general, while English uses the bare noun without “the.” The article still matches the noun: la vida, la paciencia, el tiempo.
Fingiendo is the -iendo form of fingir and presents pretending as an activity in progress.
Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.
Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: I love; I care deeply for (a person)
cards.noteEn: Querer usually means “to want,” but when its object is a person it commonly expresses affection or love. Te quiero is often less intense than te amo, though usage varies.

example.en: I love you very much, Grandma.

cards.noteEn: Sospecha is the present form of sospechar used with él, ella, or formal usted.

cards.answerEn: I am (in a state or condition)

cards.promptEs: estar + palabra que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe how someone or something is feeling or doing at a particular time?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by a describing word for the state.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to match who or what has the state: estoy means “I am,” está means “he, she, or it is,” and están means “they are.” The describing word matches the person or thing in gender and number: enfadado, enfadada, enfadados, or enfadadas. This pattern presents the quality as a condition or state; ser is normally used for identity or a defining description.

cards.answerEn: they are going to; you all are going to (formal)
cards.noteEn: Van is the present form of ir for ellos, ellas, or formal ustedes. Before a and an unchanged action verb, it helps express what is expected to happen.

example.en: They are going to arrive tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)

cards.noteEn: Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.en: We lived there for two years.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.
